title: Die klugen Leute
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 104. Text from Wikisource („Die klugen Leute (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 104, a comic tale of a swindle answered by a bigger one. A cattle-dealer talks a none-too-sharp farmwife into handing over three cows and accepting a fourth as ‘security’ for a payment that never comes; her husband, too fond of her to give the beating he promised, sets out instead to find someone even more foolish than she is, so that she can be let off. He finds his match and more in a woman standing atop a hay-wagon hunting the load for a lost needle, whom he persuades he has just fallen from heaven and can carry money and messages to her dead husband there. Mother and son between them hand over a purse of silver and a good horse before the trick runs its course, and the farmer comes home no poorer for his wife's foolishness after all — the narrator's closing aside suggests he, for one, has learned to prize a simpleton.

sentences.t: Eines Tages holte ein Bauer seinen hagebüchnen Stock aus der Ecke und sprach zu seiner Frau „Trine, ich gehe jetzt über Land und komme erst in drei Tagen wieder zurück.
sentences.l: One day a peasant fetched his hornbeam stick out of the corner and spoke to his wife “Trine, I am going over land now and come back again only in three days.
sentences.i: One day a peasant took his hornbeam cudgel out of the corner and said to his wife: “Trine, I am off across country now, and I shall not be back for three days.
sentences.n: hagebüchen means made of hornbeam, a notoriously hard wood; the stick is the promise the rest of the tale hangs on. “über Land gehen” is to travel out of the village, across country. erst here = not before, only.

sentences.t: Wenn der Viehhändler in der Zeit bei uns einspricht und will unsere drei Kühe kaufen, so kannst du sie losschlagen, aber nicht anders als für zweihundert Thaler, geringer nicht, hörst du.“
sentences.l: If the cattle-dealer calls in on us in that time and wants to buy our three cows, then you may knock them down, but not otherwise than for two hundred Thaler, not less, do you hear.”
sentences.i: If the cattle dealer looks in on us in the meantime and wants to buy our three cows, you may let them go — but on no other terms than two hundred thaler, not a penny under, do you hear.”
sentences.n: einsprechen bei jemand is the old “to call in on someone.” losschlagen, of goods, is to sell off, to knock down. The Thaler is the standard large silver coin, so two hundred is a serious sum. “hörst du” is printed with a full stop, not a question mark.

sentences.t: „Geh nur in Gottes Namen,“ antwortete die Frau, „ich will das schon machen.“
sentences.l: “Just go in God’s name,” answered the wife, “I will manage that all right.”
sentences.i: “Go along, in God’s name,” answered the wife; “I shall see to it.”
sentences.n: “in Gottes Namen” is an everyday send-off rather than piety. schon after a verb of intention is the reassuring one: never fear, it will be done.

sentences.t: „Ja, du!“ sprach der Mann, „du bist als ein kleines Kind einmal auf den Kopf gefallen, das hängt dir bis auf diese Stunde nach.
sentences.l: “Yes, you!” spoke the man, “you fell on your head once as a small child; that hangs after you to this hour.
sentences.i: “Oh yes, you!” said the man. “You fell on your head once when you were a little child, and it has clung to you to this very hour.
sentences.n: “Ja, du!” is flat sarcasm — you, of all people. nachhängen, to cling to or trail after someone, is separable, and its particle waits at the end of the clause; the person it clings to stands in the dative, dir.

sentences.t: Aber das sage ich dir, machst du dummes Zeug, so streiche ich dir den Rücken blau an, und das ohne Farbe, bloß mit dem Stock den ich da in der Hand habe, und der Anstrich soll ein ganzes Jahr halten, darauf kannst du dich verlassen.“
sentences.l: But this I tell you: do you do foolish stuff, then I paint your back blue for you, and that without paint, merely with the stick that I have here in my hand, and the coat shall last a whole year — on that you can rely.”
sentences.i: But I tell you this: if you do anything foolish, I shall paint your back blue for you — and that without any paint, with nothing but the stick I have here in my hand; and the coat shall last a whole year, you may depend upon it.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb comes first, “machst du dummes Zeug,” and English has to supply the “if.” anstreichen, to give a coat of paint, is separable, the an at the end; dir is the dative of the person it is done to. The joke runs on through Anstrich, the coat of paint, which is the beating.

sentences.t: Damit gieng der Mann seiner Wege.
sentences.l: With that the man went his ways.
sentences.i: With that the man went on his way.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging. “seiner Wege gehen” is a fixed phrase with an old genitive, literally to go of one’s ways.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen kam der Viehhändler, und die Frau brauchte mit ihm nicht viel Worte zu machen.
sentences.l: On the next morning the cattle-dealer came, and the wife needed not to make many words with him.
sentences.i: The next morning the cattle dealer came, and the wife had no need to waste many words on him.
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” = on the next morning; ander here is next, not other. “nicht viel Worte machen” is to make no long business of a thing.

sentences.t: Als er die Kühe besehen hatte und den Preis vernahm, sagte er „das gebe ich gerne, so viel sind sie unter Brüdern werth.
sentences.l: When he had looked the cows over and heard the price, he said “that I give gladly, that much they are worth among brothers.
sentences.i: When he had looked the cows over and heard the price he said: “I will give that gladly; they are worth as much as that between friends.
sentences.n: “unter Brüdern” — among brothers — is the dealer’s phrase for a fair price with no haggling, what a thing is worth between friends. vernehmen is to hear, to learn of.

sentences.t: Ich will die Thiere gleich mitnehmen.“
sentences.l: I will take the animals along at once.”
sentences.i: I shall take the beasts along at once.”
sentences.n: Thiere is the 1857 spelling of Tiere. mitnehmen is separable; in the infinitive the particle is glued back on the front.

sentences.t: Er machte sie von der Kette los und trieb sie aus dem Stall.
sentences.l: He made them loose from the chain and drove them out of the stall.
sentences.i: He unfastened them from the chain and drove them out of the byre.
sentences.n: losmachen is to make loose, to untie: the cows stand tethered by a chain in the stall. Stall is any beast-house, here the cow-house.

sentences.t: Als er eben zum Hofthor hinaus wollte, faßte ihn die Frau am Ermel und sprach „ihr müßt mir erst die zweihundert Thaler geben, sonst kann ich Euch nicht gehen lassen.“
sentences.l: When he was just about to go out at the yard-gate, the wife took hold of him by the sleeve and spoke “you must give me the two hundred Thaler first, otherwise I cannot let you go.”
sentences.i: Just as he was making off out of the yard gate, the wife caught him by the sleeve and said: “You must give me the two hundred thaler first, or I cannot let you go.”
sentences.n: Ermel is the 1857 spelling of Ärmel, sleeve. “wollte hinaus” — wollen with a bare word of direction and no verb of motion: wanted out. The polite plural wavers between small ihr and capital Euch inside one speech, as the 1857 text prints it.

sentences.t: „Richtig,“ antwortete der Mann, „ich habe nur vergessen meine Geldkatze umzuschnallen.
sentences.l: “Right,” answered the man, “I have only forgotten to buckle on my money-belt.
sentences.i: “Quite right,” answered the man; “I have simply forgotten to buckle on my money belt.
sentences.n: Die Geldkatze is the long belt-purse worn buckled round the waist under the coat — the traveller’s wallet. umschnallen is separable, and in the zu-infinitive the zu slips inside the verb: um-zu-schnallen.

sentences.t: Aber macht Euch keine Sorge, ihr sollt Sicherheit haben, bis ich zahle.
sentences.l: But make yourselves no worry, you shall have security until I pay.
sentences.i: But do not trouble yourself; you shall have security until I pay.
sentences.n: Sicherheit here is the legal word: security, something held against payment. macht is the plural imperative, the polite ihr again.

sentences.t: Zwei Kühe nehme ich mit und die dritte lasse ich Euch zurück, so habt Ihr ein gutes Pfand.“
sentences.l: Two cows I take along and the third I leave you behind, so you have a good pledge.”
sentences.i: I shall take two cows along and leave you the third, so that you have a good pledge.”
sentences.n: The object comes first — “Zwei Kühe nehme ich mit” — and the verb still stands second, which is German’s ordinary way of putting weight on the front word. zurücklassen is separable, the particle at the end. Pfand is the thing left in pawn.

sentences.t: Der Frau leuchtete das ein, sie ließ den Mann mit seinen Kühen abziehen und dachte „wie wird sich der Hans freuen, wenn er sieht daß ich es so klug gemacht habe.“
sentences.l: To the wife that shone in; she let the man draw off with his cows and thought “how will the Hans rejoice when he sees that I have done it so cleverly.”
sentences.i: The wife saw the sense of it, let the man make off with his cows, and thought: “How pleased Hans will be when he sees how cleverly I have managed it.”
sentences.n: einleuchten, to be evident to someone, is literally to shine in, and the person convinced stands in the dative: der Frau. The definite article before a name — “der Hans” — is familiar spoken German and does not carry over into English.

sentences.t: Der Bauer kam den dritten Tag, wie er gesagt hatte, nach Haus und fragte gleich ob die Kühe verkauft wären.
sentences.l: The peasant came on the third day, as he had said, home and asked at once whether the cows were sold.
sentences.i: The peasant came home on the third day, as he had said, and asked at once whether the cows were sold.
sentences.n: “den dritten Tag” is a bare accusative of time — on the third day, with no preposition. wären is subjunctive because the question is reported.

sentences.t: „Freilich, lieber Hans,“ antwortete die Frau, „und wie du gesagt hast, für zweihundert Thaler.
sentences.l: “Certainly, dear Hans,” answered the wife, “and as you said, for two hundred Thaler.
sentences.i: “To be sure, dear Hans,” answered the wife, “and just as you said, for two hundred thaler.
sentences.n: freilich = of course, to be sure.

sentences.t: So viel sind sie kaum werth, aber der Mann nahm sie ohne Widerrede.“
sentences.l: That much they are hardly worth, but the man took them without contradiction.”
sentences.i: They are hardly worth so much, but the man took them without a word of argument.”
sentences.n: Widerrede is a speaking-against, an objection; “ohne Widerrede” is without demur. werth is the 1857 spelling of wert.

sentences.t: „Wo ist das Geld?“ fragte der Bauer.
sentences.l: “Where is the money?” asked the peasant.
sentences.n: The question and its speech tag are held together as one unit here, the way the tale prints them.

sentences.t: „Das Geld das habe ich nicht,“ antwortete die Frau, „er hatte gerade seine Geldkatze vergessen, wirds aber bald bringen; er hat mir ein gutes Pfand zurück gelassen.“
sentences.l: “The money — that I do not have,” answered the wife, “he had just forgotten his money-belt but will bring it soon; he has left me a good pledge behind.”
sentences.i: “The money — that I have not got,” answered the wife; “he had just forgotten his money belt, but he will bring it soon. He has left me a good pledge.”
sentences.n: “Das Geld das habe ich nicht” names the topic first and then picks it up again with das, a spoken-German turn that the 1857 text leaves unpunctuated. wirds = wird es.

sentences.t: „Was für ein Pfand?“ fragte der Mann.
sentences.l: “What kind of a pledge?” asked the man.
sentences.n: “was für ein” = what sort of a; für here is not for, and the case of the noun is settled by its own clause, not by für.

sentences.t: „Eine von den drei Kühen, die kriegt er nicht eher, als bis er die andern bezahlt hat.
sentences.l: “One of the three cows — that one he does not get sooner than until he has paid for the others.
sentences.i: “One of the three cows; he does not get her until he has paid for the others.
sentences.n: Eine is feminine, standing in for eine Kuh. “nicht eher, als bis” is a doubled construction — not sooner than until — where English says it once.

sentences.t: Ich habe es klug gemacht, ich habe die kleinste zurück behalten, die frißt am wenigsten.“
sentences.l: I have done it cleverly, I have kept the smallest back, that one eats the least.”
sentences.i: I managed it cleverly: I kept the smallest back, for she eats the least.”
sentences.n: fressen is the verb for an animal’s eating, essen for a person’s. The 1857 text prints zurück behalten as two words where modern spelling has zurückbehalten.

sentences.t: Der Mann ward zornig, hob seinen Stock in die Höhe und wollte ihr damit den verheißenen Anstrich geben.
sentences.l: The man became wrathful, lifted his stick into the height and wanted to give her the promised coat with it.
sentences.i: The man grew angry, raised his stick, and was minded to give her the promised coat of paint with it.
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, modern wurde. “in die Höhe heben” is to lift up. verheißen, to promise, is an elevated word, and the Anstrich promised is the beating of the first paragraph.

sentences.t: Plötzlich ließ er ihn sinken und sagte „du bist die dummste Gans, die auf Gottes Erdboden herum wackelt, aber du dauerst mich.
sentences.l: Suddenly he let it sink and said “you are the stupidest goose that waddles about on God’s earth, but you move me to pity.
sentences.i: All at once he let it drop and said: “You are the stupidest goose that waddles about on God’s earth — but I am sorry for you.
sentences.n: “du dauerst mich” puts the persons the other way round from English: you are the subject and I the object, and it means I feel pity for you. Gans as an insult for a woman is as old and as blunt in German as in English.

sentences.t: Ich will auf die Landstraße gehen und drei Tage lang warten ob ich Jemand finde, der noch einfältiger ist als du bist.
sentences.l: I will go out onto the highroad and wait three days long whether I find someone who is still simpler than you are.
sentences.i: I shall go out to the highroad and wait three days to see whether I can find anyone still simpler than you.
sentences.n: einfältig — simple in the head, silly — is the word the whole tale turns on, and the ironic “klugen Leute” of the title. “warten ob” with no verb of seeing between: waiting to see whether.

sentences.t: Glückt mirs, so sollst du frei sein, finde ich ihn aber nicht, so sollst du deinen wohl verdienten Lohn ohne Abzug erhalten.“
sentences.l: Does it succeed for me, then you shall be free; but do I not find him, then you shall receive your well-deserved wages without deduction.”
sentences.i: If I succeed you shall go free; but if I do not find him, you shall have your well-earned wages without any deduction.”
sentences.n: Two more verb-first conditionals in a row: “Glückt mirs …”, “finde ich ihn aber nicht …”, each answered by so. mirs = mir es. “Lohn ohne Abzug” is a wage-payer’s phrase, pay in full with nothing kept back, and here it means the whole beating.

sentences.t: Er gieng hinaus auf die große Straße, setzte sich auf einen Stein und wartete auf die Dinge, die kommen sollten.
sentences.l: He went out onto the great road, set himself down on a stone and waited for the things that were to come.
sentences.i: He went out to the highroad, sat down on a stone, and waited for whatever might come.
sentences.n: “sich setzen” — to set oneself — is the ordinary German for to sit down. sollten here is what is due or destined to happen, not obligation.

sentences.t: Da sah er einen Leiterwagen heran fahren, und eine Frau stand mitten darauf, statt auf dem Gebund Stroh zu sitzen, das dabei lag, oder neben den Ochsen zu gehen und sie zu leiten.
sentences.l: Then he saw a ladder-wagon come driving up, and a woman stood in the middle upon it, instead of sitting on the truss of straw that lay there, or of going beside the oxen and leading them.
sentences.i: Then he saw a ladder wagon come driving up, and a woman standing in the middle of it instead of sitting on the truss of straw that lay there, or walking beside the oxen and leading them.
sentences.n: A Leiterwagen is the open farm wagon whose sides are ladder-frames. heranfahren is separable and is printed here as two words around the infinitive. Both zu-clauses hang from the single statt.

sentences.t: Der Mann dachte „das ist wohl eine, wie du sie suchst,“ sprang auf und lief vor dem Wagen hin und her, wie einer der nicht recht gescheidt ist.
sentences.l: The man thought “that is surely one such as you are looking for,” sprang up and ran to and fro in front of the wagon, like one who is not quite right in the head.
sentences.i: The man thought: “Here, surely, is one of the sort you are looking for,” and he sprang up and ran to and fro in front of the wagon like a man not right in his wits.
sentences.n: He thinks of himself as du, which German does easily in inward speech. gescheidt is the 1857 spelling of gescheit, clever or sound in the head; “nicht recht gescheidt” is not quite right in the head.

sentences.t: „Was wollt ihr Gevatter,“ sagte die Frau zu ihm, „ich kenne euch nicht, von wo kommt Ihr her?“
sentences.l: “What do you want, Gevatter,” said the wife to him, “I do not know you, from where do you come?”
sentences.i: “What do you want, good neighbour?” the woman said to him. “I do not know you — where do you come from?”
sentences.n: Gevatter is properly the godparent bond between two households, but it is also, as here, a familiar way of addressing a strange man; the nearest English is a friendly “neighbour.” “von wo … her” splits the compound woher across the clause.

sentences.t: „Ich bin von dem Himmel gefallen,“ antwortete der Mann, „und weiß nicht wie ich wieder hin kommen soll; könnt ihr mich nicht hinauf fahren?“
sentences.l: “I have fallen from heaven,” answered the man, “and do not know how I am to get there again; can you not drive me up?”
sentences.i: “I have fallen out of heaven,” answered the man, “and do not know how I am to get back there again. Can you not drive me up?”
sentences.n: der Himmel is both sky and heaven, and the joke lives on the two senses at once. hinkommen is to get there; hin points away from the speaker, her towards.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ sagte die Frau, „ich weiß den Weg nicht.
sentences.l: “No,” said the wife, “I do not know the way.
sentences.n: weiß here is the verb wissen, to know a fact, not the colour.

sentences.t: Aber wenn Ihr aus dem Himmel kommt, so könnt Ihr mir wohl sagen wie es meinem Mann geht, der schon seit drei Jahren dort ist:
sentences.l: But if you come out of heaven, then you can surely tell me how it goes with my husband, who has been there three years already:
sentences.i: But if you come from heaven, then you can surely tell me how my husband does, who has been there these three years:
sentences.n: “wie es jemandem geht” — how it goes with someone — is the standing German for how someone is. The present tense ist with seit does the work of an English perfect: has been.

sentences.t: Ihr habt ihn gewis gesehen?“
sentences.l: You have certainly seen him?”
sentences.i: You will surely have seen him?”
sentences.n: gewis is the 1857 spelling of gewiß. It is a statement with a question mark: she takes it for granted.

sentences.t: „Ich habe ihn wohl gesehen, aber es kann nicht allen Menschen gut gehen.
sentences.l: “I have indeed seen him, but it cannot go well for all people.
sentences.i: “I have seen him right enough, but things cannot go well for everybody.
sentences.n: wohl here concedes: yes, I have. The impersonal es … gehen again, with the people in the dative.

sentences.t: Er hütet die Schafe, und das liebe Vieh macht ihm viel zu schaffen, das springt auf die Berge und verirrt sich in der Wildnis, und da muß er hinterher laufen und es wieder zusammen treiben.
sentences.l: He tends the sheep, and the dear cattle make him much to do; it springs onto the mountains and loses itself in the wilderness, and then he must run after it and drive it together again.
sentences.i: He tends the sheep, and the dear beasts give him a great deal of trouble: they run up the mountains and stray in the wild, and he has to run after them and drive them together again.
sentences.n: “zu schaffen machen” is to give trouble. Vieh is a neuter singular collective, so German says das … das … es where English must go plural. hinterher laufen and zusammen treiben are both separable and printed as two words in 1857.

sentences.t: Abgerissen ist er auch, und die Kleider werden ihm bald vom Leib fallen.
sentences.l: Ragged he is too, and the clothes will soon fall from his body.
sentences.i: He is in rags, too, and the clothes will soon fall off his body.
sentences.n: abgerissen, literally torn off, said of a person means out at elbows, in rags; standing first it carries the emphasis. ihm is a dative of possession: his body.

sentences.t: Schneider gibt es dort nicht, der heil. Petrus läßt keinen hinein, wie Ihr aus dem Märchen wißt.“
sentences.l: Tailors there are none there, the holy Peter lets none in, as you know from the tale.”
sentences.i: There are no tailors there: Saint Peter lets none of them in, as you know from the story.”
sentences.n: “der heil.” is the printed abbreviation of der heilige, Saint. The tale pointed at is the one about the tailor thrown out of heaven, and the teller assumes her hearer knows it. “es gibt” with the noun first: tailors, there are none.

sentences.t: „Wer hätte sich das gedacht!“ rief die Frau, „wißt Ihr was?
sentences.l: “Who would have thought that!” cried the wife, “do you know what?
sentences.i: “Who would ever have thought it!” cried the woman. “Do you know what?
sentences.n: “sich etwas denken” has a reflexive dative — to think a thing to oneself, to imagine it. hätte … gedacht is the past subjunctive.

sentences.t: ich will seinen Sonntagsrock holen, der noch daheim im Schrank hängt, den kann er dort mit Ehren tragen.
sentences.l: I will fetch his Sunday coat, which still hangs at home in the cupboard; that he can wear there with honour.
sentences.i: I shall fetch his Sunday coat, which still hangs at home in the cupboard: he can wear that there with credit.
sentences.n: The Sonntagsrock, the good coat kept for church, is a labouring man’s one valuable garment. “den kann er … tragen” puts the object first again, with the demonstrative den pointing back to the coat.

sentences.t: Ihr seid so gut und nehmt ihn mit.“
sentences.l: You are so good and take him along.”
sentences.i: Be so good as to take it along.”
sentences.n: “seid so gut und …” — be so good and — is the ordinary polite request, where German coordinates and English subordinates. ihn is the coat, masculine Rock, which English has to turn into it.

sentences.t: „Das geht nicht wohl,“ antwortete der Bauer, „Kleider darf man nicht in den Himmel bringen, die werden einem vor dem Thor abgenommen.“
sentences.l: “That will hardly do,” answered the peasant, “clothes one may not bring into heaven, they are taken from one before the gate.”
sentences.i: “That will hardly do,” answered the peasant. “Clothes may not be brought into heaven; they are taken from you at the gate.”
sentences.n: man and its dative einem are the indefinite one. abnehmen, to take from, is separable, and the person deprived stands in the dative. Thor is the 1857 spelling of Tor.

sentences.t: „Hört mich an,“ sprach die Frau, „ich habe gestern meinen schönen Weizen verkauft und ein hübsches Geld dafür bekommen, das will ich ihm schicken.
sentences.l: “Hear me out,” spoke the wife, “I sold my fine wheat yesterday and got a pretty money for it, that I will send him.
sentences.i: “Listen to me,” said the woman. “I sold my fine wheat yesterday and got a tidy sum for it, and that I mean to send him.
sentences.n: anhören, to hear out, is separable, with the an at the end. “ein hübsches Geld” — a pretty money — treats Geld as a countable sum: a tidy amount.

sentences.t: Wenn Ihr den Beutel in die Tasche steckt, so wirds kein Mensch gewahr.“
sentences.l: If you stick the purse into your pocket, then no person becomes aware of it.”
sentences.i: If you put the purse in your pocket, no one will be any the wiser.”
sentences.n: “gewahr werden” is to become aware of something; wirds = wird es, the es being what nobody notices. kein Mensch = nobody at all.

sentences.t: „Kanns nicht anders sein,“ erwiderte der Bauer, „so will ich Euch wohl den Gefallen thun.“
sentences.l: “Can it not be otherwise,” replied the peasant, “then I will indeed do you the favour.”
sentences.i: “If it cannot be otherwise,” replied the peasant, “then I will do you the favour.”
sentences.n: Another conditional with the verb in front and no wenn: if it cannot be otherwise. Kanns = kann es; thun is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: „Bleibt nur da sitzen,“ sagte sie, „ich will heim fahren und den Beutel holen; ich bin bald wieder hier.
sentences.l: “Just stay sitting there,” said she, “I will drive home and fetch the purse; I am soon back here again.
sentences.i: “Only stay sitting there,” she said; “I shall drive home and fetch the purse — I shall soon be back.
sentences.n: bleiben takes a bare infinitive where English uses a participle: stay sitting. nur softens the imperative to just, only.

sentences.t: Ich setze mich nicht auf das Bund Stroh, sondern stehe auf dem Wagen, so hats das Vieh leichter.“
sentences.l: I do not set myself on the bundle of straw, but stand on the wagon, so the cattle have it easier.”
sentences.i: I shall not sit down on the truss of straw but stand on the wagon, and that way the beasts have it easier.”
sentences.n: Her kindness is the joke: her weight is on the wagon either way. das Bund is a bundle or truss, the same thing the tale called Gebund a few lines earlier. hats = hat es.

sentences.t: Sie trieb ihre Ochsen an, und der Bauer dachte, „die hat Anlage zur Narrheit, bringt sie das Geld wirklich, so kann meine Frau von Glück sagen, denn sie kriegt keine Schläge.“
sentences.l: She drove her oxen on, and the peasant thought, “that one has a disposition to folly; brings she the money really, then my wife can speak of luck, for she gets no blows.”
sentences.i: She urged her oxen on, and the peasant thought: “There is a natural gift for folly. If she really brings the money, my wife may count herself lucky, for she will get no beating.”
sentences.n: antreiben is separable. “Anlage zu etwas” is the inborn bent or aptitude for a thing, and said of folly it is the driest joke in the tale. “von Glück sagen” is to be able to call oneself lucky. One more verb-first conditional: “bringt sie das Geld wirklich.”

sentences.t: Es dauerte nicht lange, so kam sie gelaufen, brachte das Geld und steckte es ihm selbst in die Tasche.
sentences.l: It did not last long, then she came running, brought the money and stuck it into his pocket herself.
sentences.i: It was not long before she came running, brought the money, and put it into his pocket with her own hand.
sentences.n: “es dauerte nicht lange, so …” = it was not long before. “kam gelaufen” — came in a running state — is how German says came running, with the past participle after kommen.

sentences.t: Eh sie weggieng, dankte sie ihm noch tausendmal für seine Gefälligkeit.
sentences.l: Before she went away, she thanked him yet a thousand times for his obligingness.
sentences.i: Before she went off she thanked him a thousand times over for his kindness.
sentences.n: Eh is the short form of ehe, before. weggieng is the 1857 spelling of wegging, from separable weggehen.

sentences.t: Als die Frau wieder heim kam, so fand sie ihren Sohn, der aus dem Feld zurück gekehrt war.
sentences.l: When the wife came home again, so she found her son, who had come back from the field.
sentences.i: When the woman came home again she found her son, who had come back from the field.
sentences.n: The so at the head of the main clause after an als-clause is an old resumptive; English simply leaves it out.

sentences.t: Sie erzählte ihm was sie für unerwartete Dinge erfahren hätte und setzte dann hinzu „ich freue mich recht daß ich Gelegenheit gefunden habe, meinem armen Mann etwas zu schicken, wer hätte sich vorgestellt, daß er im Himmel an etwas Mangel leiden würde?“
sentences.l: She told him what unexpected things she had learned and then added “I am right glad that I have found opportunity to send my poor husband something; who would have imagined that he would suffer want of anything in heaven?”
sentences.i: She told him what unlooked-for news she had had, and then added: “I am truly glad to have found a chance of sending my poor husband something. Who would have imagined that he should want for anything in heaven?”
sentences.n: “was sie für … Dinge” is the was für frame pulled apart: what sort of things. hätte and würde are subjunctive because this is her report and not the narrator’s claim. hinzusetzen, to add, is separable; “an etwas Mangel leiden” is to suffer want of something.

sentences.t: Der Sohn war in der größten Verwunderung, „Mutter,“ sagte er, „so einer aus dem Himmel kommt nicht alle Tage, ich will gleich hinaus und sehen daß ich den Mann noch finde:
sentences.l: The son was in the greatest astonishment. “Mother,” said he, “such a one out of heaven does not come every day, I will out at once and see that I still find the man:
sentences.i: The son was in the greatest astonishment. “Mother,” said he, “one from heaven does not come every day. I shall go straight out and see whether I can still find the man:
sentences.n: “ich will gleich hinaus” is wollen with a bare word of direction and no verb of motion — I want out — which English cannot copy. “sehen daß …” is to see to it that.

sentences.t: der muß mir erzählen wies dort aussieht und wies mit der Arbeit geht.“
sentences.l: he must tell me what it looks like there and how it goes with the work.”
sentences.i: he must tell me what it is like there and how the work goes.”
sentences.n: wies = wie es, twice over. aussehen is separable. The der at the head is the demonstrative, that one, he — not a relative pronoun.

sentences.t: Er sattelte das Pferd und ritt in aller Hast fort.
sentences.l: He saddled the horse and rode away in all haste.
sentences.n: fortreiten is separable, the fort standing at the end. “in aller Hast” = in all haste.

sentences.t: Er fand den Bauer, der unter einem Weidenbaum saß und das Geld, das im Beutel war, zählen wollte.
sentences.l: He found the peasant, who sat under a willow tree and wanted to count the money that was in the purse.
sentences.i: He found the peasant sitting under a willow tree, about to count the money that was in the purse.
sentences.n: wollen is often on the point of, about to, rather than a stated wish: he was just going to count it.

sentences.t: „Habt Ihr nicht den Mann gesehen,“ rief ihm der Junge zu, „der aus dem Himmel gekommen ist?“
sentences.l: “Have you not seen the man,” the lad called to him, “who has come out of heaven?”
sentences.i: “Have you not seen the man,” the lad called out to him, “who came from heaven?”
sentences.n: zurufen, to call to someone, is separable and takes the person in the dative: ihm. The relative clause is held back to the far side of the speech tag.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete der Bauer, „der hat sich wieder auf den Rückweg gemacht und ist den Berg dort hinauf gegangen, von wo ers etwas näher hat.
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered the peasant, “he has made himself onto the way back again and has gone up the mountain there, from where he has it somewhat nearer.
sentences.i: “Yes,” answered the peasant; “he has set out on his way back and has gone up the mountain there, from where it is a shorter way for him.
sentences.n: “sich auf den Weg machen” is to set out. ers = er es; “es näher haben” is to have the shorter distance to go.

sentences.t: Ihr könnt ihn noch einholen, wenn Ihr scharf reitet.“
sentences.l: You can still catch him up if you ride sharply.”
sentences.i: You may still overtake him if you ride hard.”
sentences.n: einholen, to catch up with, is separable. “scharf reiten” is to ride hard.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sagte der Junge, „ich habe mich den ganzen Tag abgeäschert, und der Ritt hierher hat mich vollends müde gemacht:
sentences.l: “Ah,” said the lad, “I have worn myself out the whole day, and the ride here has made me quite tired:
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the lad, “I have worked myself to a rag the whole day, and the ride out here has finished me:
sentences.n: sich abäschern is an old regional verb — to wear oneself down to ashes, to slave — and is rare enough that its exact force here has to be read from the situation. “den ganzen Tag” is a bare accusative of time. vollends = quite, on top of everything.

sentences.t: Ihr kennt den Mann, seid so gut und setzt Euch auf mein Pferd und überredet ihn daß er hierher kommt.“
sentences.l: You know the man, be so good and set yourself on my horse and persuade him that he comes here.”
sentences.i: You know the man: be so good as to get on my horse and persuade him to come here.”
sentences.n: kennen is to know a person, wissen to know a fact. Another “seid so gut und …” request. überreden takes a daß-clause where English uses an infinitive: persuade him to come.

sentences.t: „Aha,“ meinte der Bauer, „das ist auch einer, der keinen Dacht in seiner Lampe hat.“
sentences.l: “Aha,” said the peasant, “that is another one who has no wick in his lamp.”
sentences.i: “Aha,” observed the peasant, “here is another with no wick in his lamp.”
sentences.n: Dacht is an old form of Docht, the wick. No wick in the lamp — nothing there to give light — is the tale’s own image rather than a standing German idiom, and it lands as oddly in German as in English. meinen here is to say by way of an opinion.

sentences.t: „Warum sollte ich Euch den Gefallen nicht thun?“ sprach er, stieg auf und ritt im stärksten Trab fort.
sentences.l: “Why should I not do you the favour?” he spoke, mounted up and rode away at the strongest trot.
sentences.i: “Why should I not do you the favour?” said he, mounted, and rode off at a smart trot.
sentences.n: aufsteigen, to mount, is separable. “im stärksten Trab” is as fast as the beast will trot.

sentences.t: Der Junge blieb sitzen bis die Nacht einbrach, aber der Bauer kam nicht zurück.
sentences.l: The lad stayed sitting until the night broke in, but the peasant did not come back.
sentences.i: The lad sat there until night fell, but the peasant did not come back.
sentences.n: einbrechen, said of night, is to fall, to break in.

sentences.t: „Gewis,“ dachte er, „hat der Mann aus dem Himmel große Eile gehabt und nicht umkehren wollen, und der Bauer hat ihm das Pferd mitgegeben, um es meinem Vater zu bringen.“
sentences.l: “Certainly,” thought he, “the man from heaven has had great haste and not wanted to turn back, and the peasant has given him the horse along, to bring it to my father.”
sentences.i: “No doubt,” he thought, “the man from heaven was in great haste and would not turn back, and the peasant gave him the horse to take to my father.”
sentences.n: “nicht umkehren wollen” is the double infinitive: wollen takes the place of a past participle but keeps the infinitive’s form. mitgeben, to give along with someone, is separable.

sentences.t: Er gieng heim und erzählte seiner Mutter was geschehen war: das Pferd habe er dem Vater geschickt, damit er nicht immer herum zu laufen brauche.
sentences.l: He went home and told his mother what had happened: the horse he had sent to his father, so that he should not always have to run about.
sentences.i: He went home and told his mother what had happened: he had sent the horse to his father, so that he should not always have to go about on foot.
sentences.n: habe and brauche are subjunctive I, the mark of reported speech — this is what the lad said, and the narrator stands clear of it. brauchen with zu is to need to.

sentences.t: „Du hast wohl gethan,“ antwortete sie, „du hast noch junge Beine und kannst zu Fuß gehen.“
sentences.l: “You have done well,” answered she, “you still have young legs and can go on foot.”
sentences.i: “You did right,” she answered; “you have young legs still and can go on foot.”
sentences.n: gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan. She answers as though the horse had been the son’s to give.

sentences.t: Als der Bauer nach Haus gekommen war, stellte er das Pferd in den Stall neben die verpfändete Kuh, gieng dann zu seiner Frau und sagte „Trine, das war dein Glück, ich habe zwei gefunden, die noch einfältigere Narren sind als du:
sentences.l: When the peasant had come home, he put the horse in the stall beside the pledged cow, went then to his wife and said “Trine, that was your luck, I have found two who are still simpler fools than you:
sentences.i: When the peasant had come home he put the horse in the byre beside the pledged cow, then went to his wife and said: “Trine, that was your good fortune. I have found two who are simpler fools still than you:
sentences.n: verpfändet is from Pfand, a pledge: the cow left behind as security. “das war dein Glück” = that was your good luck, lucky for you.

sentences.t: diesmal kommst du ohne Schläge davon, ich will sie für eine andere Gelegenheit aufsparen.“
sentences.l: this time you come off without blows, I will save them up for another occasion.”
sentences.i: this time you get off without a beating; I shall save it up for another occasion.”
sentences.n: davonkommen, to get off or escape, and aufsparen, to save up, are both separable. Schläge is plural where English says a beating.

sentences.t: Dann zündete er seine Pfeife an, setzte sich in den Großvaterstuhl und sprach „das war ein gutes Geschäft, für zwei magere Kühe ein glattes Pferd und dazu einen großen Beutel voll Geld.
sentences.l: Then he lit his pipe, set himself in the grandfather-chair and spoke “that was a good piece of business, for two lean cows a sleek horse and on top of that a great purse full of money.
sentences.i: Then he lit his pipe, sat down in the grandfather chair, and said: “That was a good bargain — a sleek horse for two lean cows, and a great purse full of money into the bargain.
sentences.n: anzünden is separable. Der Großvaterstuhl is the high-backed armchair by the stove. glatt, said of a horse, is sleek, in good coat.

sentences.t: Wenn die Dummheit immer so viel einbrächte, so wollte ich sie gerne in Ehren halten.“
sentences.l: If stupidity always brought in so much, then I would gladly hold it in honour.”
sentences.i: If stupidity always brought in as much as that, I would gladly hold it in honour.”
sentences.n: einbrächte and wollte are both past subjunctive, marking the condition as unreal. einbringen, to bring in or yield, is separable, and wollen here carries the English would rather than a wish.

sentences.t: So dachte der Bauer, aber dir sind gewis die einfältigen lieber.
sentences.l: So thought the peasant, but to you the simple ones are surely dearer.
sentences.i: So thought the peasant; but you, no doubt, like the simple ones better.
sentences.n: In its last clause the tale turns and addresses the reader directly as du, the only time it does so. “dir sind die einfältigen lieber” has the person who prefers in the dative and lieber, dearer, doing the work: you like the simple folk better. A sly last word, since the klugen Leute of the title are the ones who come off worst.

glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; also ‘he/she’ for neuter nouns such as das Kind, das Mädchen)
glossary.gekehrt: zurückkehren — returned (past participle, printed “zurück gekehrt”; separable zurück-)
glossary.geschickt: schicken — sent (past participle); not geschickt, skilful
glossary.gevatter: der Gevatter — godfather; also a familiar way of addressing a strange man, roughly neighbour
glossary.halten: halten — to hold; of a thing, to last, to hold up (infinitive)
glossary.heil: heilig — holy, Saint (the 1857 text prints the abbreviation “der heil.” for der heilige)
glossary.hört: anhören — hear (2nd pl. imperative, printed “hört … an”: hear me out); also hören, hears
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, for him; to it (dative)
glossary.ja: ja — yes; also a flavouring particle, surely, after all
glossary.leuchtete: einleuchten — was plain, was evident to (3rd sg. past, printed “leuchtete … ein”; separable ein-, person in the dative)
glossary.lieber: lieb — dearer, preferred (comparative; “mir ist … lieber”: I like … better); also lieber, dear (inflected)
glossary.losschlagen: losschlagen — to sell off, to knock down (of goods; infinitive, separable los-)
glossary.müßt: müssen — must, have to (2nd pl. present; 1857 spelling of müsst)
glossary.sage: sagen — (I) say, tell (1st sg. present); not die Sage, legend
glossary.setzte: setzen — set, put (3rd sg. past; sich setzen: sat down; hinzu setzen: added)
glossary.streiche: anstreichen — (I) paint, give a coat of paint (1st sg. present; separable an-)
glossary.weiß: wissen — to know (1st and 3rd sg. present); also weiß, white (adj.)
